title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 14: Ethics in the Biotechnological Revolution
keywords: ability is not equivalent to permissibility
primary_topics: Chapter 14 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's forum address arguing that ethics begins where capability ends, since the ability to do something does not equate with entitlement to do so, and applying that divide to the biotechnological revolution.

His taxonomy of the three sources from which ethical answers come -- religious belief, human nature as read by philosophy, and human covenant -- each examined in turn for what it can and cannot settle about the new sciences.

His account of the polarization the revolution has produced: a freewheeling libertarian camp that would place no limits on bioscientific development, and a camp calling for restraint on religious, philosophical, moral, environmental, social and cultural grounds.

His survey of proposed responses -- Francis Fukuyama's call for regulation, particularly international regulation, and EINSHAC's proposed International Science and Technology Reference Forum (I/STREF) of science-knowledgeable jurists rendering non-binding but persuasive opinions.
sub_topics: He states the premise: ability is not equivalent to permissibility, and between 'I can do it' and 'I may do it' lies the divide known as morality or ethics, illustrated by the man who can fire a gun and the woman who can give birth.

He turns the premise into questions about the biosciences -- whether the ability to modify organisms entitles us to feed the world that way, whether re-engineering human cells automatically empowers scientists to improve medicine, whether manipulating the embryo licenses unrestricted use of the new sciences against diabetes, cancer, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, whether science should be limited at all, and whether it would be ethical to clone humans.

He observes that as the revolution accelerates the questions grow more complex and the need for answers more urgent, so that religion, philosophy and law take center stage, with responses varying by intellectual, spiritual, economic, social, cultural and even medical circumstance.

Religion as a source: from ancient voodooism and the pluralistic deism of the Greeks, Romans, Incas, Aztecs and Chinese to the three Mosaic religions and their shared Ten Commandments, and the Christian summary in loving God and loving one another.

He traces the Catholic pro-life and anti-abortion theology protecting life from the union of sperm and ovum, quoting Pope John Paul II that the mere probability that a human person is involved would justify an absolutely clear prohibition of any intervention aimed at killing a human embryo, and noting that more fervent advocates cite Psalm 139 to reject all artificial birth control.

Philosophy as a source: beginning with human ends, from James Watson's response to needs like food, education and health, through Jeremy Bentham's utilitarianism reduced to the pursuit of pleasure and escape from pain.

He sets against utilitarianism the scholastic insistence on rationality and dignity, illustrated by the comatose accident victim whose healthy liver may not be excised for a revered leader or great scientist, because the lesser mortal holds rights no one can take without his consent even in the guise of the greater good.

He connects individual rights to liberal democracy and constitutional law, where the awesome might of the state, even backed by an overwhelming majority, cannot prevail over the fundamental rights of a single individual.

He concedes the weakness of the rights approach: rights abound and conflict, the right to life is livid with controversy between unborn and mother, and procreative liberty collides frontally with the scientist's claimed right to re-engineer people genetically.

Human covenant as the third and, on this proposition, authoritative source: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, given constitutional force in his country as a generally accepted principle of international law, the covenants on economic and social rights, civil and political rights and the rights of the child, and, nationally, professional codes of ethics and an Ethical Standards Law for government officials.

He closes on the polarization between the libertarian and the restraint camps, and on the two proposed answers -- Fukuyama's regulation, ranging from industry self-regulation with minimal oversight to formal government regulation, and EINSHAC's I/STREF, a private, voluntary, non-binding body of jurists and law-oriented scientists whose opinions would be persuasive enough to be accepted.

stances.claim: Ethics rests on the premise that ability is not entitlement: between 'I can do it' and 'I may do it' lies the divide known as morality or ethics, and the biotechnological revolution must be judged on that divide.
stances.rhetorical_move: definitional opening with homely illustrations -- the man who can fire a gun, the woman who can give birth -- to make an abstract principle concrete before applying it to science

stances.claim: Ethical answers about the new sciences come from three separate sources -- religious belief, human nature, and human covenant -- and because rights claims proliferate and conflict, there is a proposition that the truly authoritative source is human covenant.
stances.rhetorical_move: tripartite taxonomy, each source examined and found partial, with the third introduced as the response to the confusion in the intellectual marketplace

stances.claim: Individual human dignity limits utilitarian calculation: the healthy organ of an unlamented accident victim may not be taken for a revered leader or great scientist, because his rights cannot be removed without his consent even in the guise of promoting the far greater good.
stances.rhetorical_move: hard-case hypothetical: he stages the most tempting possible trade-off and refuses it, to show that dignity outranks aggregate benefit

stances.claim: Faced with the polarization between the libertarian and restraint camps, the way forward lies in some form of regulation or consultative body, whether Fukuyama's international regulation or EINSHAC's non-binding but persuasive I/STREF.
stances.rhetorical_move: presenting two named proposals side by side and declining to choose, while insisting the ethical questions be discussed in every forum

notable_anecdotes: The transplant hypothetical: he imagines the healthy liver of a comatose reckless driver being excised for a revered political leader or great scientist, and refuses it as a violation of the lesser mortal's dignity.

Pope John Paul II on the embryo: he quotes the Pope that the mere probability that a human person is involved would suffice to justify an absolutely clear prohibition of any intervention aimed at killing a human embryo.

Psalm 139 and birth control: he notes that avid pro-life advocates, citing that Yahweh knew them before birth in the womb, shun the diaphragm, the condom and the pill as preventing a conception the Lord has willed.

The I/STREF proposal: he describes EINSHAC's plan for a private, voluntary body of science-knowledgeable jurists sitting with law-oriented scientists, to whom national tribunals or litigants could refer their consultas for a legally non-binding but persuasive opinion.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 14 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' is CJP's forum address on ethics in the biotechnological revolution, built on the premise that the ability to do something does not equate with entitlement to do so -- ability is not equivalent to permissibility, and between 'I can do it' and 'I may do it' lies the divide known as morality or ethics. He applied that divide to a cascade of questions: whether the power to modify organisms entitles us to feed the world that way, whether re-engineering human cells automatically empowers scientists to improve medicine, whether the capacity to manipulate the embryo permits unrestricted use of the new sciences against diabetes, cancer, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, whether science should be limited at all, and, ultimately, whether it would be ethical to clone humans. Answers, he said, come from three separate sources. Religion has always exerted an enduring influence on human conduct, from ancient voodooism and pluralistic deism to the Ten Commandments shared by the Mosaic faiths and the Christian summary of loving God and one another, out of which grew the Catholic pro-life theology quoted from Pope John Paul II, that the mere probability a human person is involved justifies an absolutely clear prohibition of any intervention aimed at killing an embryo. Philosophy begins with human ends -- James Watson's needs and wants, Bentham's utilitarian pleasure and pain -- but the insistence on rationality leads instead to dignity, which is why, in his hypothetical, the healthy liver of a comatose reckless driver may not be taken for a revered leader, since rights cannot be removed without consent even in the guise of the greater good; this premise, he added, underwrites liberal democracy and constitutional law, though rights proliferate and conflict, as when procreative liberty collides with the scientist's claimed right to re-engineer people. Because of that confusion, a third proposition holds that the truly authoritative source of ethics is human covenant -- the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the covenants on civil, economic and children's rights, professional codes and his country's Ethical Standards Law. He closed on the polarization between the libertarian and restraint camps and on two proposed responses, Fukuyama's call for regulation, particularly international regulation, and EINSHAC's I/STREF, insisting that either way these ethical questions are worth discussing in every forum of the dawning bio-age.
